items.stem: Distinguish between the natural greenhouse effect and the enhanced greenhouse effect.

items.stem: Suggest why Arctic temperatures have risen about four times faster than the global average since 1979.
items.answer: Arctic amplification: loss of sea ice lowers albedo; open water absorbs more energy; changes in atmospheric heat transport and a shallower boundary layer concentrate warming.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "albedo"?
options: The movement of carbon between stores (atmosphere, oceans, biosphere, soils, lithosphere) through flows such as photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition and combustion
A gas that absorbs and emits longwave radiation, e.g. water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide
High-energy radiation emitted by the Sun, mostly visible light and ultraviolet, that passes easily through the atmosphere
The proportion of incoming solar radiation reflected by a surface, from 0 (none) to 1 (all); fresh snow about 0.8-0.9, ocean about 0.06
items.answer: The proportion of incoming solar radiation reflected by a surface, from 0 (none) to 1 (all); fresh snow about 0.8-0.9, ocean about 0.06
items.markingKey: D. "albedo" is the proportion of incoming solar radiation reflected by a surface, from 0 (none) to 1 (all); fresh snow about 0.8-0.9, ocean about 0.06.

items.stem: Explain why high-latitude regions have an energy deficit and the tropics a surplus.
items.answer: At high latitudes the Sun's rays strike at a low angle and pass through more atmosphere, so energy is spread over a larger area, and snow/ice albedo is high; the tropics receive more concentrated radiation all year. Winds and ocean currents transfer the surplus poleward.

items.stem: Explain how water vapour acts as a feedback rather than a forcing.
items.answer: Warmer air holds about 7% more water vapour per °C (Clausius-Clapeyron); extra vapour absorbs more longwave radiation, amplifying warming caused by other forcings, but it does not stay long enough in the air to drive change on its own.

items.stem: Incoming shortwave radiation is 180 W/m². A surface of asphalt road (albedo 0.05) is replaced by cropland (albedo 0.2). Calculate the change in absorbed radiation and explain its significance for climate feedbacks.

items.markingKey: M1 (1 − albedo) × incoming for both; A1 171.0 and 144.0; A1 change -27.0 W/m²; R1 feedback explained.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Indonesia's 2015 peat-fire crisis shows land-use change as a source of greenhouse gases.
items.answer: Fires on drained peatlands released an estimated 1.5 Gt CO₂-equivalent and created a regional haze. Draining carbon-rich peat for plantations turned a store into a large source.
items.markingKey: Context (Fires on drained peatlands released an estimated 1.5 Gt CO₂-equivalent and created a regional haze.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Draining carbon-rich peat for plantations turned a store into a large source. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to land-use change as a source of greenhouse gases.

Study the resource below.

Diagram description (simplified global energy budget, W/m²): incoming solar 340; reflected by clouds and atmosphere 77; reflected by the surface 23; absorbed by the atmosphere 79; absorbed by the surface 161.

items.stem: "Responsibility for climate change should be based on historical emissions rather than current emissions." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Both matter: historical emissions justify greater obligations for early industrialisers, but all major current emitters must cut.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - arguments supporting the statement: the USA and EU account for a large share of cumulative CO₂ since 1850; principle of common but differentiated responsibilities. Arguments challenging it: current emitters (China, India) will determine future warming; past emitters could not know the effects before the 1980s. Evaluation should weigh places, scales, perspectives and time. Judgement: Both matter: historical emissions justify greater obligations for early industrialisers, but all major current emitters must cut. items.stem: Examine the view that the natural greenhouse effect is more significant for life on Earth than the enhanced greenhouse effect.
items.answer: The natural effect is far larger, but the enhanced effect matters more for future human well-being.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: it raises temperatures by about 33 °C and enables liquid water; human additions so far have added about 1.1-1.3 °C. Against / limitations: the enhanced effect is changing climate rapidly with large impacts on people; small changes in mean temperature have big effects on extremes. items.stem: "Feedback loops are a greater threat to the global climate than direct human emissions." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Human emissions are the root cause; feedbacks magnify them, so cutting emissions is the way to avoid crossing tipping points.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - arguments supporting the statement: permafrost, ice-albedo and forest dieback could add warming beyond human control; tipping points may be irreversible. items.stem: State what is meant by the term "albedo".
items.answer: The proportion of incoming solar radiation reflected by a surface, from 0 (none) to 1 (all); fresh snow about 0.8-0.9, ocean about 0.06
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the proportion of incoming solar radiation reflected by a surface, from 0 (none) to 1 (all); fresh snow about 0.8-0.9, ocean about 0.06. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "climate forcing"?
options: The additional warming caused by human emissions of greenhouse gases that increase their atmospheric concentration
The warming of the Earth's surface because greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit outgoing longwave radiation, raising the mean temperature from about −18 °C to about +15 °C
A change that alters the Earth's energy balance (in W/m²), such as changes in solar output, aerosols or greenhouse gases
A carbon-rich energy source (coal, oil, natural gas) formed from ancient organic matter, releasing CO₂ when burned
items.answer: A change that alters the Earth's energy balance (in W/m²), such as changes in solar output, aerosols or greenhouse gases
items.markingKey: C. "climate forcing" is a change that alters the Earth's energy balance (in W/m²), such as changes in solar output, aerosols or greenhouse gases.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The movement of carbon between stores (atmosphere, oceans, biosphere, soils, lithosphere) through flows such as photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition and combustion"?
items.answer: carbon cycle
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of carbon cycle.

items.stem: Priya writes: "The greenhouse effect is entirely harmful." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The natural greenhouse effect is essential for life; it is the human-enhanced effect that is causing dangerous warming.
items.markingKey: The natural greenhouse effect is essential for life; it is the human-enhanced effect that is causing dangerous warming. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Climate has always changed, so current change must be natural." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Past changes had natural causes, but current warming is far faster than most past changes and matches the fingerprint of rising greenhouse gases from fossil fuels.
items.markingKey: Past changes had natural causes, but current warming is far faster than most past changes and matches the fingerprint of rising greenhouse gases from fossil fuels. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Omar writes: "Carbon dioxide is the only greenhouse gas that humans emit." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Humans also emit methane, nitrous oxide and fluorinated gases, which together contribute about a quarter of current warming.
items.markingKey: Humans also emit methane, nitrous oxide and fluorinated gases, which together contribute about a quarter of current warming. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between longwave radiation and shortwave radiation.
items.answer: Shortwave radiation comes from the hot Sun and passes through the atmosphere; longwave (infrared) radiation is emitted by the cooler Earth and is absorbed by greenhouse gases.
items.markingKey: Shortwave radiation comes from the hot Sun and passes through the atmosphere; longwave (infrared) radiation is emitted by the cooler Earth and is absorbed by greenhouse gases. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between natural climate forcing and anthropogenic climate forcing.
items.answer: Natural forcings include solar variation, orbital cycles and volcanic aerosols; anthropogenic forcings include greenhouse-gas emissions, aerosols and land-use change.
items.markingKey: Natural forcings include solar variation, orbital cycles and volcanic aerosols; anthropogenic forcings include greenhouse-gas emissions, aerosols and land-use change. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between a carbon store and a carbon flux.
items.answer: A store is a reservoir that holds carbon (e.g. the ocean holds about 38,000 GtC); a flux is the transfer of carbon between stores (e.g. photosynthesis, combustion).
items.markingKey: A store is a reservoir that holds carbon (e.g. the ocean holds about 38,000 GtC); a flux is the transfer of carbon between stores (e.g. photosynthesis, combustion). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using Arctic sea ice as an example, explain the ice-albedo effect.
items.answer: September sea-ice extent has declined by about 13% per decade since satellite records began in 1979. Replacing bright ice (albedo about 0.6) with dark ocean (about 0.06) increases absorption of solar energy.
items.markingKey: Context (September sea-ice extent has declined by about 13% per decade since satellite records began in 1979.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Replacing bright ice (albedo about 0.6) with dark ocean (about 0.06) increases absorption of solar energy. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the ice-albedo effect.

items.stem: Between 2004 and 2024 the area of Arctic summer (September) sea ice measured by a polar research centre changed from 7.4 to 5.0 million km². Calculate the percentage change over the period.
items.markingKey: M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100 = (5.0 − 7.4) ÷ 7.4 × 100; A1 -32.4% (sign or "increase/decrease" required).

items.stem: Using data, compare the CO₂ emissions of a high-income country and a low-income country.
items.answer: e.g. the USA emits about 4.9 Gt (about 14.5 t per person) and Ethiopia about 0.02 Gt (about 0.15 t per person): over 90 times more per person, reflecting energy use, industry and transport.

items.stem: Using the Maunder Minimum (about 1645-1715) as an example, explain solar forcing of climate.
items.answer: Very few sunspots coincided with part of the Little Ice Age in Europe. A reduction in solar activity is associated with cooler conditions, though volcanic activity also contributed.
items.markingKey: Context (Very few sunspots coincided with part of the Little Ice Age in Europe.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.markingKey: M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100 = (66.0 − 47.7) ÷ 47.7 × 100; A1 +38.4% (sign or "increase/decrease" required).

items.stem: A city replaces dark asphalt roofs (albedo 0.05) with white roofs (albedo 0.7). Explain the likely effect on local temperatures.
items.answer: Higher albedo reflects much more incoming radiation, so roofs absorb less energy and emit less heat, reducing the urban heat island and indoor cooling demand.
items.markingKey: Higher albedo reflects much more incoming radiation, so roofs absorb less energy and emit less heat, reducing the urban heat island and indoor cooling demand.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that land-use change is now a more important human cause of climate change than burning fossil fuels.
items.answer: Fossil fuels are by far the dominant cause; land-use change is significant mainly in a few tropical countries.
